case.case_title: Jeevakaran v. Ratnasiri Wickremanayake and Others
case.source_citation: Supreme Court of Sri Lanka, S.C. Application No. 623/96, decided on 28 January 1997

clause.text: No citizen shall be discriminated against on the grounds of race, religion, language, caste, sex, political opinion, place of birth or any one of such grounds.

case_context.legal_issue: Whether the removal of Maha Sivarathri and Hadji public holidays constituted discrimination against minority religions in violation of Article 12(2).
case_context.petitioner_claim: The petitioner argued that removing holidays only from minority religions while not reducing holidays for majority religions amounted to discrimination prohibited by Article 12(2).
case_context.respondent_argument: The Government contended that the decision was based on legitimate economic reasons and was not discriminatory. The grant of special holidays for the affected minority religions further negated any claim of discrimination.
key_facts: Maha Sivarathri and Hadji holidays were removed while some holidays for majority religions remained.
Special holidays were declared for followers of Hinduism and Islam after removal.
The Government acted on recommendations to reduce excessive public holidays affecting productivity.
The petitioner claimed discrimination based on religion.
The Minister had statutory power to vary the public holiday schedule.

reasoning.interpretation_summary: The Court held that Article 12(2) prohibits discrimination but the Government's decision was a legitimate exercise of discretion considering multiple factors. The reduction of holidays was not based on religious discrimination but on economic and national interests. The special holidays granted mitigated any potential discrimination.
reasoning.application_to_facts: The Court found no evidence that the Government acted with improper purpose or arbitrariness. The petitioner failed to prove that the removal of holidays was discriminatory under Article 12(2).
principles_established: Article 12(2) prohibits discrimination but allows for reasonable government discretion.
Economic and productivity considerations can justify differential treatment in public holidays.
Special holidays can address concerns of minority religious groups.
Statutory powers to vary holidays are relevant to assessing discrimination claims.

outcome.holding: The Court dismissed the petitioner's claim that Article 12(2) was violated by the removal of Maha Sivarathri and Hadji as public holidays.

link_explanation.why_this_clause_matters: Article 12(2) was directly invoked by the petitioner to claim religious discrimination. The Court's analysis of discrimination and the legitimacy of government discretion made this clause central to the decision.

evidence.evidence_excerpt: It is quite clear that the Government did not intend to discriminate against followers of Hinduism and Islam. The material adduced by the petitioner is quite insufficient to show that the elimination of these two holidays was unreasonable, arbitrary, capricious or for an improper purpose.
